Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on debentures
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about interest on debentures:
(A) It is calculated on the face (nominal) value of the debentures.
(B) It is payable even if the company incurs a loss.
(C) It is debited to the Statement of Profit and Loss as a finance cost.
(D) When debentures are issued at a discount, interest is calculated on the issue price.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Interest is a fixed obligation calculated on the face value (A). It is a charge against profit, payable irrespective of profit or loss (B), and is shown under Finance costs in the Statement of Profit and Loss (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the issue price (discount or premium) never changes the interest base, which is always the face value. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Interest = Face value × Coupon rate × Time.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account — preparation
questions.question: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account of a partnership firm is prepared:
options: A) After preparing the Profit and Loss Account
B) Before preparing the Trading Account
C) Instead of the Profit and Loss Account
D) Only when the firm suffers a loss
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) After preparing the Profit and Loss Account
Why: The Profit and Loss Account works out the net profit after all charges. The Appropriation Account then begins with that net profit and shows how it is divided — interest on capital, salary, commission, transfer to reserve and the partners' shares.
Why not the others:
(B) The Trading Account comes first, then the P&L Account, then the Appropriation Account.
(C) It is an extension of the P&L Account, not a substitute for it.
(D) It is prepared every year, whether there is a profit or a loss.
Key point: Trading A/c → P&L A/c → P&L Appropriation A/c.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Treatment of amounts received on issue of shares
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Amount)
(A) Excess application money of applicants allotted pro-rata
(B) Premium received on the issue of shares
(C) Calls received before they are due
(D) Application money on rejected applications

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Adjusted towards the allotment money
(II) Credited to the Securities Premium Account
(III) Credited to the Calls in Advance Account
(IV) Refunded to the applicants

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Pro-rata applicants' excess money is normally adjusted towards allotment (and calls) → (I).
(B) Premium on issue goes to Securities Premium under Section 52 → (II).
(C) Money received before a call is due is a liability → Calls in Advance (III).
(D) Applicants who get no shares are paid back in full → (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the pro-rata and rejected-application treatments; (C) swaps premium and calls in advance; (D) swaps pro-rata excess and calls in advance.
Key point: Rejected → refund; pro-rata excess → adjust; advance → liability; premium → Securities Premium.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Commission to a partner based on sales
questions.question: A firm's profit before partners' commission is ₹2,00,000. Partner A is entitled to a commission of 5% on the firm's sales, which were ₹8,00,000 during the year. The profit left for distribution in the profit-sharing ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,60,000
Given: The basis of the commission is SALES, not profit.
Step 1: Commission = 5% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹40,000
Step 2: Divisible profit = ₹2,00,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹1,60,000
Common mistake: Calculating 5% on profit (₹10,000) gives ₹1,90,000 (A). Forgetting the commission gives ₹2,00,000 (C). Using 10% on sales gives ₹1,20,000 (D).
Key point: Always read the basis of the commission carefully — profit before commission, profit after commission, or sales.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares — minimum subscription
questions.question: As per SEBI guidelines, the minimum subscription that must be received in a public issue before the company can allot shares is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 90% of the issue
Why: SEBI requires a company to receive at least 90% of the issue amount as minimum subscription. If it fails to do so, the entire application money must be refunded within the prescribed time.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not the prescribed limit; full subscription is not required.
Key point: Below 90% → no allotment, refund all application money.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Calls in advance — interest (Table F)
questions.question: A shareholder holding 1,000 shares paid the final call of ₹4 per share three months before it was due. The company follows Table F, which allows interest on calls in advance at 12% p.a. The interest payable to him is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹120
Step 1: Calls in advance = 1,000 × ₹4 = ₹4,000
Step 2: Interest = ₹4,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹120 (debited to Interest on Calls in Advance, a finance cost)
Common mistake: Using the calls-in-arrears rate of 10% gives ₹100 (A). Charging a full year gives ₹480 (B). Counting 4 months gives ₹160 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — ratio of old partners when not specified
questions.question: When a new partner is admitted and nothing is said about how he acquires his share, it is assumed that the old partners will share future profits among themselves in:
options: D) The sacrificing ratio of the previous admission
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Their old ratio
Why: When the agreement is silent, the new partner is taken to acquire his share from the old partners in their old ratio. Their mutual ratio therefore stays unchanged, and their sacrificing ratio equals their old ratio.
Why not the others:
(A) Equal sharing applies when there is no deed at all, not to this assumption.
(C) Capital contribution does not decide profit shares unless agreed.
(D) A previous admission has no bearing on the current one.
Key point: Silent agreement → old partners keep their old mutual ratio; sacrificing ratio = old ratio.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — modes of payment to the retiring partner
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding payment to a retiring partner:
(A) The amount due may be paid in a lump sum.
(B) The amount due may be paid in instalments with interest.
(C) If the amount is not settled immediately, he is entitled under Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, at his option, to interest at 6% p.a. or to a share of the profits earned by using his money.
(D) He must always be paid in full on the date of retirement.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The partners may settle the retiring partner's dues at once (A), or transfer them to his Loan Account to be paid in instalments with interest (B). Where the dues remain unsettled and there is no agreement, Section 37 lets him claim either interest at 6% p.a. or a share of the profits attributable to his money (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — immediate full payment is not compulsory, which is why the Loan Account exists. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Unpaid dues → Loan A/c, with interest as agreed (or under Section 37).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Allotment money — default including premium
questions.question: A company allotted 10,000 shares on which ₹5 per share was due on allotment (including a premium of ₹2). The holder of 500 shares failed to pay the allotment money. The cash received on allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹47,500
Step 1: Allotment due = 10,000 × ₹5 = ₹50,000
Step 2: Unpaid = 500 × ₹5 = ₹2,500 (premium included)
Step 3: Cash received = ₹50,000 − ₹2,500 = ₹47,500
Common mistake: ₹50,000 (B) ignores the default. Treating only the ₹3 capital part as unpaid gives ₹48,500 (C). Counting only the capital part of the receipts gives ₹28,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — withdrawal of premium by old partners
questions.question: The old partners decide to withdraw in cash the premium for goodwill brought in by the new partner, which has already been credited to their Capital Accounts. The entry for the withdrawal is:
options: A) Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr.; To Cash A/c
B) Cash A/c Dr.; To Old Partners' Capital A/cs
C) Old Partners' Capital A/cs Dr.; To Cash/Bank A/c
D) New Partner's Capital A/c Dr.; To Cash A/c
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Old Partners' Capital A/cs Dr.; To Cash/Bank A/c
Why: The premium was credited to the sacrificing partners' Capital Accounts. When they take it out in cash, their capitals decrease (debit) and cash goes out (credit).
Why not the others:
(A) The Premium for Goodwill A/c was already closed when it was transferred to the partners.
(B) This is the reverse entry — money coming in.
(D) The new partner withdraws nothing.
Key point: Premium brought → credit the sacrificing partners; premium withdrawn → debit them.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — premium for goodwill
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On admission, the new partner's Capital Account is credited with the premium for goodwill that he brings in.
Reason (R): Premium for goodwill belongs to the old partners who sacrifice their share of profit.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
Why: The premium is compensation to the old partners for the share of profits they give up (the Reason is true). So it is credited to the SACRIFICING partners' Capital Accounts in the sacrificing ratio — not to the new partner, who receives nothing for it. The Assertion is false.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) treat the Assertion as true.
Key point: New partner's capital = only the capital he brings; the premium goes to the sacrificing partners.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — equity shares
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about equity shareholders:
(A) They bear the highest risk in a company.
(B) The rate of dividend they receive varies with the company's profits.
(C) They normally have voting rights on all matters.
(D) On winding up, their capital is repaid before preference share capital.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Equity shareholders are the residual owners. They are paid last, so they bear the highest risk (A); their dividend depends on the profits and the board's decision (B); and they control the company through voting rights (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — preference share capital is repaid BEFORE equity capital on winding up. Options (A), (B) and (C) all include (D).
Key point: Equity = highest risk, residual reward, full control.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of profit — deficiency borne in an agreed ratio
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. C is guaranteed a minimum profit of ₹1,00,000. Any deficiency is to be borne by A and B in the ratio 3 : 1 (not their profit-sharing ratio). The firm's profit is ₹4,00,000. B's final share of profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,55,000
Step 1: Normal shares: A ₹1,60,000; B ₹1,60,000; C ₹80,000
Step 2: Deficiency = ₹1,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹20,000, borne 3 : 1 → A ₹15,000; B ₹5,000
Step 3: B's final share = ₹1,60,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹1,55,000 (A ₹1,45,000; C ₹1,00,000; total ₹4,00,000 ✔)
Common mistake: Ignoring the guarantee gives ₹1,60,000 (A). Sharing the deficiency in the profit ratio (equally between A and B) gives ₹1,50,000 (B). Charging B with A's ₹15,000 gives ₹1,45,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — share of goodwill by capitalisation of super profit
questions.question: A partner with a 2/5th share died. The firm's average profit is ₹1,50,000 and its capital employed is ₹10,00,000; the normal rate of return is 12%. Goodwill is to be valued by capitalising the super profit. The deceased partner's share of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,00,000
Step 1: Normal profit = 12% × ₹10,00,000 = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Super profit = ₹1,50,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹30,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹30,000 × 100/12 = ₹2,50,000
Step 4: Deceased partner's share = ₹2,50,000 × 2/5 = ₹1,00,000 (credited to his Capital A/c; debited to the remaining partners in their gaining ratio)
Common mistake: ₹2,50,000 (B) is the firm's goodwill. Taking 2/5 of the super profit gives ₹12,000 (C). Taking 2/5 of two years' purchase of super profit gives ₹24,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — salary allowed and ratio applied wrongly
questions.question: The profit of ₹1,20,000 for the year was distributed between A and B in the ratio 2 : 1 after allowing B a salary of ₹24,000. It was later found that the deed provides NO salary and EQUAL sharing of profits. Capitals are fixed. The single adjusting entry is:
options: A) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To A's Current A/c ₹4,000
B) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹24,000; To B's Current A/c ₹24,000
C) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹8,000; To B's Current A/c ₹8,000
D) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To B's Current A/c ₹4,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To B's Current A/c ₹4,000
Step 1: Amounts actually credited: B = salary ₹24,000 + 1/3 of ₹96,000 = ₹56,000; A = 2/3 of ₹96,000 = ₹64,000
Step 2: Correct amounts (no salary, equal shares): ₹60,000 each
Step 3: Differences: A was over-credited by ₹4,000; B was under-credited by ₹4,000
Step 4: Entry: A's Current A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To B's Current A/c ₹4,000
Common mistake: Reversing the direction gives (A). Reversing only the salary gives (B). Doubling the difference gives (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Under-subscription
questions.question: A company offered 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, with ₹3 payable on application. Applications were received for 46,000 shares, which is above the minimum subscription, and all of them were allotted. The amount transferred from the Share Application Account to the Share Capital Account is:
options: D) Nil, as the issue is under-subscribed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,38,000
Why: When an issue is under-subscribed but the minimum subscription (90% = 45,000 shares) is met, the company allots the shares actually applied for.
Step 1: Application money received = 46,000 × ₹3 = ₹1,38,000
Step 2: Entry: Share Application A/c Dr. ₹1,38,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹1,38,000
Common mistake: Using the 50,000 shares offered gives ₹1,50,000 (A). ₹12,000 (C) is the shortfall. Refunding everything (D) applies only if the minimum subscription is NOT received.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Pro-rata allotment — shares issued at a premium
questions.question: Shares of ₹10 each were issued at a premium of ₹1, payable ₹4 on application (including the premium) and ₹4 on allotment. Ram applied for 1,200 shares and was allotted 800 shares on a pro-rata basis. His excess application money was adjusted towards allotment. The cash received from Ram on allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,600
Step 1: Application money paid = 1,200 × ₹4 = ₹4,800; required for 800 shares = ₹3,200; excess = ₹1,600
Step 2: Allotment due = 800 × ₹4 = ₹3,200
Step 3: Cash payable on allotment = ₹3,200 − ₹1,600 = ₹1,600
Common mistake: Ignoring the excess gives ₹3,200 (A). Valuing the excess at the capital part of ₹3 per share (₹1,200) gives ₹2,000 (C). ₹4,800 (D) is his total application money.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — new ratio when fractions of shares are surrendered
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 5 : 3. They admit C. A surrenders 1/5th of HIS share and B surrenders 1/3rd of HIS share in favour of C. The new profit-sharing ratio of A, B and C is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2 : 1 : 1
Step 1: A surrenders 1/5 × 5/8 = 1/8 → A's new share = 5/8 − 1/8 = 4/8
Step 2: B surrenders 1/3 × 3/8 = 1/8 → B's new share = 3/8 − 1/8 = 2/8
Step 3: C's share = 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8
Step 4: New ratio = 4 : 2 : 2 = 2 : 1 : 1
Common mistake: Counting only A's surrender gives 4 : 3 : 1 (B). Counting only B's surrender gives 5 : 2 : 1 (C). Assuming equal shares gives 1 : 1 : 1 (D).
Key point: '1/5th of HIS share' means a fraction of the partner's own share, not of the whole firm.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — deceased partner's capital account
questions.question: On the death of a partner, which of the following is NOT credited to his Capital Account?
options: B) His share of profit up to the date of death
C) Interest on his capital up to the date of death
D) His drawings during the year
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) His drawings during the year
Why: Drawings reduce what is owed to the partner, so they are DEBITED to his Capital Account. Goodwill, profit up to death and interest on capital increase his claim, so they are credited.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are all amounts due TO the deceased partner and appear on the credit side.
Key point: Credits — capital, goodwill, profit, interest, reserves; debits — drawings, interest on drawings, losses.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares for consideration other than cash — promoters
questions.question: A company issued fully paid equity shares of ₹50,000 at par to its promoters for their services in forming the company. The entry is:
options: A) Goodwill (or Incorporation Costs) A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹50,000
B) Share Capital A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To Promoters' A/c ₹50,000
C) Promoters' A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To Bank A/c ₹50,000
D) Securities Premium A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹50,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Goodwill (or Incorporation Costs) A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹50,000
Why: The promoters are paid for their services in shares instead of cash. The value of the services is debited (NCERT debits Goodwill or Incorporation Costs) and Share Capital is credited. This is an issue for consideration other than cash.
Why not the others:
(B) This reduces capital, whereas an issue increases it.
(C) No cash is paid.
(D) This is not a use of Securities Premium permitted for this purpose.
Key point: Shares for services or assets → debit what is received, credit Share Capital (and Securities Premium if issued at a premium).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital — capital withdrawn during the year
questions.question: On 1 April 2025, Kiran's capital was ₹3,00,000. On 1 January 2026 he withdrew ₹60,000 out of his capital (not as drawings against profit). Interest on capital is allowed at 8% p.a., and the books are closed on 31 March 2026. Interest on Kiran's capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹22,800
Step 1: ₹3,00,000 from 1 April to 31 December (9 months): ₹3,00,000 × 8% × 9/12 = ₹18,000
Step 2: ₹2,40,000 from 1 January to 31 March (3 months): ₹2,40,000 × 8% × 3/12 = ₹4,800
Step 3: Total = ₹18,000 + ₹4,800 = ₹22,800
Common mistake: Ignoring the withdrawal gives ₹24,000 (A). Applying the reduced capital for the whole year gives ₹19,200 (B). Averaging the capital at ₹2,70,000 gives ₹21,600 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account — transfer to reserve
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 2 : 1. After allowing interest on capital and salary, the profit of the firm is ₹1,50,000. The deed requires 10% of this profit to be transferred to General Reserve before distribution. A's share of profit will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹90,000
Step 1: Transfer to General Reserve = 10% × ₹1,50,000 = ₹15,000 (debited to the P&L Appropriation A/c)
Step 2: Divisible profit = ₹1,50,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹1,35,000
Step 3: A's share = ₹1,35,000 × 2/3 = ₹90,000 (B ₹45,000)
Common mistake: Ignoring the transfer gives ₹1,00,000 (B). Dividing equally gives ₹67,500 (C). Deducting the reserve twice (₹30,000) gives ₹80,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital after forfeiture and partial re-issue
questions.question: A company issued and allotted 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called up. 1,000 shares, on which ₹4 per share had been paid, were forfeited. Of these, 600 shares were re-issued as fully paid. The amount shown under 'Share Capital' (subscribed and fully paid, plus the forfeited shares account) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹4,97,600
Step 1: Fully paid shares = 49,000 (never forfeited) + 600 (re-issued) = 49,600 × ₹10 = ₹4,96,000
Step 2: Forfeited shares not re-issued = 400; the amount received on them stays in Share Forfeiture A/c = 400 × ₹4 = ₹1,600
Step 3: Share Capital = ₹4,96,000 + ₹1,600 = ₹4,97,600
Common mistake: ₹5,00,000 (A) ignores the forfeiture. Leaving out the forfeited shares account gives ₹4,96,000 (B). Ignoring both the re-issue and the forfeited amount gives ₹4,90,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — capitalisation method with non-trade investments
questions.question: A firm's total assets are ₹7,00,000, which include non-trade investments of ₹50,000. Its outside liabilities are ₹1,50,000. The average profit is ₹75,000, which includes ₹5,000 income from the non-trade investments. The normal rate of return is 10%. Goodwill by the capitalisation of average profit method is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,00,000
Why: Non-trade investments are not used in the business, so both the investments and their income are excluded.
Step 1: Capital employed = ₹7,00,000 − ₹50,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹5,00,000
Step 2: Normal (business) average profit = ₹75,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹70,000
Step 3: Capitalised value = ₹70,000 × 100/10 = ₹7,00,000
Step 4: Goodwill = ₹7,00,000 − ₹5,00,000 = ₹2,00,000
Common mistake: Not removing the investment income gives ₹7,50,000 − ₹5,00,000 = ₹2,50,000 (A). Including the investments in capital employed (₹5,50,000) gives ₹1,50,000 (B). ₹50,000 (D) is the value of the investments.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation — unrecorded assets and liabilities
questions.question: At the time of reconstitution: building is to be appreciated by ₹40,000; unrecorded investments worth ₹10,000 are to be brought into the books; a provision of ₹8,000 is to be made for a claim for damages against the firm; and furniture is to be written down by ₹5,000. The profit or loss on revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Profit ₹37,000
Step 1: Gains: building ₹40,000 + unrecorded investments ₹10,000 = ₹50,000
Step 2: Losses: claim for damages ₹8,000 + furniture ₹5,000 = ₹13,000
Step 3: Net = profit ₹37,000
Common mistake: Treating the claim as a gain gives ₹53,000 (A). Ignoring the unrecorded investments gives ₹27,000 (B). Ignoring the claim gives ₹45,000 (C).
Key point: Unrecorded asset → gain; unrecorded liability or claim → loss.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — conditions
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Interest on drawings is charged from partners only if the partnership deed provides for it.
Reason (R): Interest on drawings is an income for the firm.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: The Assertion is true because Section 13 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not provide for interest on drawings, so it can be charged only under an agreement. The Reason is also true — interest on drawings is a gain to the firm, credited to the P&L Appropriation Account. But being income for the firm is NOT why a deed is needed; the need for a deed comes from the Act's silence.
Why not the others: (A) wrongly links the two statements. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: In A-R questions, check both the truth of each statement and the logical link between them.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — Workmen Compensation Reserve
questions.question: A, B and C share profits equally. C retires. The balance sheet shows a Workmen Compensation Reserve of ₹30,000, against which there is a claim of ₹12,000. C's share of the reserve credited to his Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹6,000
Why: The reserve first meets the actual claim; only the EXCESS is undistributed profit belonging to all the partners.
Step 1: Workmen Compensation Reserve A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To Provision for Workmen Compensation Claim ₹12,000; To Partners' Capital A/cs ₹18,000 (old ratio)
Step 2: C's share = ₹18,000 × 1/3 = ₹6,000
Common mistake: Distributing the whole reserve gives ₹10,000 (A). ₹4,000 (C) is one-third of the claim. ₹18,000 (D) is the total excess to be shared.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Accounts affected by partnership items
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II for a firm whose partners' capitals are FIXED:

List-I (Item)
(A) A partner's share of profit
(B) Additional capital introduced by a partner
(C) Interest on a partner's loan to the firm
(D) Interest on partners' drawings

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
(II) Credited to the partner's Capital Account
(III) Credited to the partner's Current Account
(IV) Debited to the Profit and Loss Account

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) With fixed capitals, routine items such as the profit share go to the Current Account → (III).
(B) A permanent change in capital goes to the Capital Account → (II).
(C) Interest on a loan is a charge → debited to the P&L Account (and credited to the partner's Loan A/c) → (IV).
(D) Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm → credited to the P&L Appropriation Account → (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the Capital and Current Accounts; (B) swaps the treatments of loan interest and interest on drawings; (D) confuses the profit share with a P&L charge.
Key point: Fixed capital → Capital A/c for permanent changes only.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — combined adjustments
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. They decide to share profits equally in future. Goodwill is valued at ₹1,80,000; General Reserve of ₹30,000 is to be distributed; and the revaluation profit is ₹12,000. The net effect of these three items on C's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Decrease of ₹23,000
Step 1: Reserve (old ratio): C = ₹30,000 × 1/6 = +₹5,000
Step 2: Revaluation profit (old ratio): C = ₹12,000 × 1/6 = +₹2,000
Step 3: Goodwill: C's gain = 1/3 − 1/6 = 1/6 → C pays ₹1,80,000 × 1/6 = −₹30,000 to the sacrificing partner
Step 4: Net effect on C = 5,000 + 2,000 − 30,000 = −₹23,000
Common mistake: Ignoring goodwill gives an increase of ₹7,000 (B). Taking only goodwill gives (C). Crediting C with goodwill instead of debiting gives an increase of ₹37,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — new ratio when the share is taken in a given proportion
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2. C retires. A takes 1/3rd of C's share and B takes the remaining 2/3rd. The new profit-sharing ratio of A and B is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 14 : 13
Step 1: C's share = 2/9; A takes 1/3 × 2/9 = 2/27; B takes 2/3 × 2/9 = 4/27
Step 2: A's new share = 4/9 + 2/27 = 12/27 + 2/27 = 14/27
Step 3: B's new share = 3/9 + 4/27 = 9/27 + 4/27 = 13/27
Step 4: New ratio = 14 : 13
Common mistake: Keeping the old ratio gives 4 : 3 (A). Splitting C's share in the old ratio instead gives 2 : 1 (B). Swapping the fractions gives 13 : 14 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — sacrificing ratio from shares surrendered
questions.question: C is admitted for a 3/10th share in profits. He takes 2/10th from A and 1/10th from B. The sacrificing ratio of A and B is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2 : 1
Why: The sacrificing ratio is the ratio of the shares actually given up.
Step 1: A gives 2/10 and B gives 1/10 → sacrificing ratio = 2/10 : 1/10 = 2 : 1
Common mistake: Assuming equal sacrifice gives 1 : 1 (A). Assuming the old ratio gives 3 : 2 (B). Reversing gives 1 : 2 (C).
Key point: When the shares surrendered are stated, those shares ARE the sacrificing ratio; the old ratio is irrelevant.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — new partner's proportionate capital
questions.question: After all adjustments on the admission of C, the capitals of A and B are ₹1,50,000 and ₹90,000. C is admitted for a 1/4th share and is required to bring capital proportionate to his share, based on the combined capital of A and B. The capital C must bring is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹80,000
Step 1: A and B together hold 3/4 of the new firm; their combined capital = ₹2,40,000
Step 2: Total capital of the new firm = ₹2,40,000 × 4/3 = ₹3,20,000
Step 3: C's capital (1/4) = ₹80,000 (or simply ₹2,40,000 × 1/3)
Common mistake: Taking 1/4 of the old partners' capital gives ₹60,000 (A). ₹2,40,000 (C) is the old partners' combined capital. Taking half of it gives ₹1,20,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares as partly paid
questions.question: 100 shares of ₹10 each (₹7 called up), on which ₹5 per share had been paid, were forfeited. They were re-issued as ₹8 paid up for ₹6 per share. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹300
Step 1: Forfeited amount = 100 × ₹5 = ₹500 (Share Capital Dr. ₹700; Calls unpaid ₹200)
Step 2: Re-issued as ₹8 paid up for ₹6 → discount = ₹2 per share = ₹200, debited to Share Forfeiture A/c
Step 3: Capital Reserve = ₹500 − ₹200 = ₹300
Common mistake: Ignoring the discount gives ₹500 (A). Measuring the discount against the original ₹7 called up (₹1 per share) gives ₹400, and ₹100 (B) is that ₹1 discount itself. ₹200 (D) is the discount, not the reserve.
Key point: Discount on re-issue = paid-up value credited to the new holder − amount received from him.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Forfeiture before all calls are made
questions.question: 300 equity shares of ₹10 each, on which ₹8 per share had been called up, were forfeited. The holder had paid only the application money of ₹3 per share. The final call had not yet been made. The amount debited to the Share Capital Account on forfeiture is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹2,400
Why: On forfeiture, Share Capital is debited with the amount CALLED UP on the shares, not their face value.
Step 1: Called up = 300 × ₹8 = ₹2,400 → Share Capital A/c Dr. ₹2,400
Step 2: Unpaid calls = 300 × ₹5 = ₹1,500 (credited to the respective call accounts); Share Forfeiture A/c Cr. = 300 × ₹3 = ₹900
Common mistake: Using face value gives ₹3,000 (A). ₹900 (B) is the forfeited amount. ₹1,500 (C) is the unpaid amount.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Debentures as collateral security — meaning
questions.question: Debentures that a company issues to a lender as an additional (secondary) security for a loan, over and above the primary security, are called:
options: C) Debentures issued as collateral security
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Debentures issued as collateral security
Why: Collateral debentures are given to the lender only as secondary security. The lender can enforce them only if the company fails to repay the loan. No money is received for them, and no interest is paid on them.
Why not the others:
(A) Convertible debentures can be converted into shares.
(B) Redeemable debentures are repayable after a period.
(D) Bearer debentures are transferable by delivery.
Key point: Collateral = secondary security for a loan; there is no real liability unless the security is enforced.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation Account — assets transferred
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. They dissolved their firm on 31 March 2026, when their balance sheet showed — Liabilities: Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹15,000; B's Loan ₹20,000; General Reserve ₹18,000; Capitals: A ₹1,00,000, B ₹60,000, C ₹40,000. Assets: Cash ₹12,000; Debtors ₹70,000; Stock ₹50,000; Furniture ₹30,000; Machinery ₹1,51,000. The assets were realised as follows: debtors ₹66,000; stock taken over by A at ₹45,000; furniture ₹24,000; machinery ₹1,40,000. Creditors accepted ₹58,000 in full settlement, bills payable were paid in full, and realisation expenses of ₹3,000 were paid by the firm.

Question: The total of the assets transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹3,01,000
Step 1: All assets except cash are transferred: Debtors ₹70,000 + Stock ₹50,000 + Furniture ₹30,000 + Machinery ₹1,51,000 = ₹3,01,000
Common mistake: Including cash gives ₹3,13,000 (A). Leaving out the stock taken over by A gives ₹2,51,000 (C); an asset taken over by a partner is still transferred first, and the partner is then debited. Adding the creditors and bills payable gives ₹3,76,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Partner's loan on dissolution
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. They dissolved their firm on 31 March 2026, when their balance sheet showed — Liabilities: Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹15,000; B's Loan ₹20,000; General Reserve ₹18,000; Capitals: A ₹1,00,000, B ₹60,000, C ₹40,000. Assets: Cash ₹12,000; Debtors ₹70,000; Stock ₹50,000; Furniture ₹30,000; Machinery ₹1,51,000. The assets were realised as follows: debtors ₹66,000; stock taken over by A at ₹45,000; furniture ₹24,000; machinery ₹1,40,000. Creditors accepted ₹58,000 in full settlement, bills payable were paid in full, and realisation expenses of ₹3,000 were paid by the firm.

Question: B's Loan of ₹20,000 will be:
options: A) Transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account
B) Transferred to B's Capital Account
C) Paid along with the partners' capitals at the very end
D) Paid in cash after the outside liabilities and before the partners' capitals
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Paid in cash after the outside liabilities and before the partners' capitals
Why: Section 48 sets the order — outside debts first, then advances (loans) by partners, then partners' capital. A partner's loan is not transferred to the Realisation Account; it is paid directly: B's Loan A/c Dr. ₹20,000; To Cash A/c ₹20,000.
Why not the others:
(A) Only OUTSIDE liabilities go to the Realisation Account.
(B) The loan is a separate claim, not part of B's capital.
(C) Loans rank ahead of capital.
Key point: Outside liabilities → partners' loans → partners' capitals.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation Account — profit or loss
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. They dissolved their firm on 31 March 2026, when their balance sheet showed — Liabilities: Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹15,000; B's Loan ₹20,000; General Reserve ₹18,000; Capitals: A ₹1,00,000, B ₹60,000, C ₹40,000. Assets: Cash ₹12,000; Debtors ₹70,000; Stock ₹50,000; Furniture ₹30,000; Machinery ₹1,51,000. The assets were realised as follows: debtors ₹66,000; stock taken over by A at ₹45,000; furniture ₹24,000; machinery ₹1,40,000. Creditors accepted ₹58,000 in full settlement, bills payable were paid in full, and realisation expenses of ₹3,000 were paid by the firm.

Question: The loss on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹27,000
Step 1: Debit side = Assets ₹3,01,000 + Creditors paid ₹58,000 + Bills payable paid ₹15,000 + Expenses ₹3,000 = ₹3,77,000
Step 2: Credit side = Creditors ₹60,000 + Bills payable ₹15,000 + Debtors ₹66,000 + Stock (A) ₹45,000 + Furniture ₹24,000 + Machinery ₹1,40,000 = ₹3,50,000
Step 3: Loss = ₹27,000, shared 3 : 2 : 1 → A ₹13,500; B ₹9,000; C ₹4,500
Common mistake: Ignoring the ₹2,000 discount from creditors gives ₹29,000 (B). Ignoring the expenses gives ₹24,000 (C). Valuing the stock taken over at book value gives ₹22,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Final settlement — partner who took over an asset
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. They dissolved their firm on 31 March 2026, when their balance sheet showed — Liabilities: Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹15,000; B's Loan ₹20,000; General Reserve ₹18,000; Capitals: A ₹1,00,000, B ₹60,000, C ₹40,000. Assets: Cash ₹12,000; Debtors ₹70,000; Stock ₹50,000; Furniture ₹30,000; Machinery ₹1,51,000. The assets were realised as follows: debtors ₹66,000; stock taken over by A at ₹45,000; furniture ₹24,000; machinery ₹1,40,000. Creditors accepted ₹58,000 in full settlement, bills payable were paid in full, and realisation expenses of ₹3,000 were paid by the firm.

Question: The cash finally paid to A in settlement of his Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹50,500
Step 1: Opening capital ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Add General Reserve share (3/6 of ₹18,000) = +₹9,000
Step 3: Less loss on realisation share (3/6 of ₹27,000) = −₹13,500
Step 4: Less stock taken over = −₹45,000
Step 5: Balance paid in cash = ₹50,500
Common mistake: Not deducting the stock gives ₹95,500 (A). Leaving out the reserve gives ₹41,500 (B). Ignoring the realisation loss gives ₹64,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Final settlement — total cash paid to partners
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. They dissolved their firm on 31 March 2026, when their balance sheet showed — Liabilities: Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹15,000; B's Loan ₹20,000; General Reserve ₹18,000; Capitals: A ₹1,00,000, B ₹60,000, C ₹40,000. Assets: Cash ₹12,000; Debtors ₹70,000; Stock ₹50,000; Furniture ₹30,000; Machinery ₹1,51,000. The assets were realised as follows: debtors ₹66,000; stock taken over by A at ₹45,000; furniture ₹24,000; machinery ₹1,40,000. Creditors accepted ₹58,000 in full settlement, bills payable were paid in full, and realisation expenses of ₹3,000 were paid by the firm.

Question: The total cash paid to the three partners in settlement of their Capital Accounts is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,46,000
Step 1: Cash inflows = Opening ₹12,000 + Debtors ₹66,000 + Furniture ₹24,000 + Machinery ₹1,40,000 = ₹2,42,000
Step 2: Cash outflows before capitals = Creditors ₹58,000 + Bills payable ₹15,000 + Expenses ₹3,000 + B's loan ₹20,000 = ₹96,000
Step 3: Balance for capitals = ₹1,46,000 (check: A ₹50,500 + B ₹57,000 + C ₹38,500 = ₹1,46,000 ✔)
Common mistake: Not paying B's loan separately gives ₹1,66,000 (A). ₹2,00,000 (C) is the original total of capitals. Treating A's stock as if it had been sold for cash gives ₹1,91,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Tools of financial analysis — trend analysis
questions.question: Expressing each year's figures as a percentage of the figures of a base year (taken as 100) is known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Trend analysis
Why: Trend analysis selects a base year (= 100) and expresses the same item in later years as percentages of it, showing the direction of change over several years — for example revenue: 100, 112, 125, 140.
Why not the others:
(A) Comparative statements show absolute and percentage changes, usually between two periods.
(B) Common-size statements use a base WITHIN one period.
(C) Ratio analysis relates different items to each other.
Key point: Base year = 100 → trend analysis.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Common-size balance sheet — interpretation
questions.question: In a company's common-size balance sheet, current assets are 40% of total assets and current liabilities are 25% of total equity and liabilities. The company's current ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.6 : 1
Why: Both percentages share the same base (total assets = total equity and liabilities), so their ratio equals the ratio of the actual amounts.
Step 1: Current ratio = 40% ÷ 25% = 1.6 : 1
Common mistake: Inverting the ratio gives 0.625 : 1 (B). Subtracting the two percentages gives 15% (C), which is the working capital as a percentage of total assets, not a ratio. 2.5 : 1 (D) has no basis in the data.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements of a company — Schedule III headings
questions.question: As per Schedule III, 'Loose tools' are shown in a company's balance sheet under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Inventories
Why: Schedule III lists the classes of inventories as raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade, stores and spares, loose tools and others. So loose tools are shown under Inventories, within Current assets.
Why not the others:
(A) PPE covers major tangible assets such as land, buildings and machinery.
(C) Other current assets covers items such as accrued income.
(D) Short-term loans and advances covers advances given.
Key point: Inventories include loose tools and stores and spares.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Accounting ratios — objectives
questions.question:
Which of the following are objectives or advantages of ratio analysis?
(A) It helps to judge a firm's liquidity, solvency and profitability.
(B) It helps in inter-firm and intra-firm comparisons.
(C) It simplifies and summarises accounting data.
(D) It removes the need for judgement in decision-making.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Ratios condense large financial statements into meaningful relationships (C), reveal the firm's liquidity, solvency, efficiency and profitability (A), and make comparisons possible across firms and over time (B).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — ratios are aids to judgement, not substitutes for it. They must be interpreted in context, along with qualitative factors. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Ratios inform decisions; they do not make them.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Accounting ratios — numerators
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ratio)
(A) Current ratio
(B) Quick ratio
(C) Proprietary ratio
(D) Interest coverage ratio

List-II (Numerator)
(I) Net profit before interest and tax
(II) Shareholders' funds
(III) Quick assets
(IV) Current assets

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities → (IV).
(B) Quick ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities → (III).
(C) Proprietary ratio = Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets → (II).
(D) Interest coverage = PBIT ÷ Interest on long-term debt → (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the two liquidity numerators; (B) swaps quick assets and shareholders' funds; (C) swaps PBIT and current assets.
Key point: Both liquidity ratios share the denominator (current liabilities); only the numerator differs.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from investing activities — investments and income
questions.question: During the year, a non-finance company purchased investments for ₹80,000, sold investments costing ₹50,000 at a profit of ₹5,000, received interest of ₹6,000 on investments and received dividend of ₹4,000. The net cash flow from investing activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹15,000 outflow
Step 1: Purchase of investments = −₹80,000
Step 2: Sale of investments = cost ₹50,000 + profit ₹5,000 = +₹55,000
Step 3: Interest received +₹6,000; dividend received +₹4,000 (both investing for a non-finance company)
Step 4: Net = −80,000 + 55,000 + 6,000 + 4,000 = −₹15,000 (outflow)
Common mistake: Taking the sale at cost (₹50,000) gives ₹20,000 outflow (A). Leaving out the interest and dividend gives ₹25,000 outflow (B). Counting the profit twice gives ₹5,000 outflow (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Liquidity ratios — quick ratio from current ratio
questions.question: A company's current ratio is 2.5 : 1 and its current assets are ₹5,00,000, of which inventory is ₹1,50,000 (there are no prepaid expenses). Its quick ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.75 : 1
Step 1: Current liabilities = ₹5,00,000 ÷ 2.5 = ₹2,00,000
Step 2: Quick assets = ₹5,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹3,50,000
Step 3: Quick ratio = ₹3,50,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000 = 1.75 : 1
Common mistake: 2.5 : 1 (A) is the current ratio. 1.5 : 1 (B) and 1.25 : 1 (D) come from deducting the inventory from the ratio itself instead of from the assets.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — income tax paid from provision for tax
questions.question: The provision for tax was ₹30,000 at the beginning of the year and ₹40,000 at the end. During the year, a provision of ₹45,000 was made for the current year. The income tax actually paid during the year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹35,000
Why: Prepare the Provision for Tax account — the opening balance plus the new provision, less the closing balance, gives the tax paid.
Step 1: Opening ₹30,000 + Provision made ₹45,000 = ₹75,000
Step 2: Less closing balance ₹40,000
Step 3: Tax paid = ₹35,000 (deducted under operating activities)
Common mistake: Taking the provision made as the tax paid gives ₹45,000 (B). ₹10,000 (C) is the increase in the provision. Adding the closing balance instead of deducting it gives ₹55,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — inventory turnover with gross profit on cost
questions.question: A trader fixes his selling price by adding 25% to cost. His revenue from operations for the year is ₹6,00,000. He began the year with stock of ₹70,000 and ended it with stock of ₹90,000. How many times did his inventory turn over during the year?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6 times
Step 1: GP of 25% on cost means Revenue = Cost × 125% → Cost of revenue = ₹6,00,000 × 100/125 = ₹4,80,000
Step 2: Average inventory = (₹70,000 + ₹90,000) ÷ 2 = ₹80,000
Step 3: Inventory turnover = ₹4,80,000 ÷ ₹80,000 = 6 times
Common mistake: Using revenue gives 7.5 times (A). Treating 25% as a margin on REVENUE (cost ₹4,50,000) gives 5.63 times (B). Using the closing inventory gives 5.33 times (D).
Key point: 25% on cost = 20% on revenue.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Profitability ratios — operating ratio
questions.question: Revenue from operations is ₹7,00,000, cost of revenue from operations is ₹4,50,000 and operating expenses are ₹75,000. The operating ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 75%
Formula: Operating ratio = (Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses) ÷ Revenue from operations × 100
Step 1: Operating cost = ₹4,50,000 + ₹75,000 = ₹5,25,000
Step 2: Operating ratio = ₹5,25,000 ÷ ₹7,00,000 × 100 = 75%
Common mistake: Using only the cost of revenue gives 64.29% (A). 25% (C) is the operating PROFIT ratio (100% − 75%). 85% (D) comes from double-counting the expenses.
Key point: Operating ratio + Operating profit ratio = 100%.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll accounting — salary components
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Payroll item)
(A) Basic pay
(B) Dearness Allowance (DA)
(C) House Rent Allowance (HRA)
(D) Professional tax

List-II (Description)
(I) Allowance to offset the rise in the cost of living
(II) Fixed core component on which several other components are based
(III) Allowance towards the rent of accommodation
(IV) Statutory deduction levied by State Governments

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Basic pay is the fixed core of salary; DA, HRA and PF are often calculated on it → (II).
(B) DA compensates for inflation → (I).
(C) HRA helps meet house rent → (III).
(D) Professional tax is a deduction imposed by State Governments → (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps basic pay and DA; (C) swaps DA and HRA; (D) swaps basic pay and professional tax.
Key point: Earnings (basic, DA, HRA) − deductions (PF, professional tax, TDS) = net pay.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll accounting — working back to gross salary
questions.question: An employee's net salary is ₹45,000. His basic pay is ₹30,000. The deductions are Provident Fund at 12% of basic pay and professional tax of ₹200. His gross salary is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹48,800
Step 1: PF = 12% × ₹30,000 = ₹3,600
Step 2: Total deductions = ₹3,600 + ₹200 = ₹3,800
Step 3: Gross salary = Net salary + Deductions = ₹45,000 + ₹3,800 = ₹48,800
Common mistake: ₹45,000 (A) is the net salary itself. Forgetting the professional tax gives ₹48,600 (B). Deducting the deductions instead of adding them gives ₹41,200 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Depreciation schedule — double-declining balance
questions.question: A depreciation schedule uses the double-declining balance (=DDB) method for an asset costing ₹80,000 with a useful life of 4 years and a negligible salvage value. The book value of the asset at the end of the second year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹20,000
Step 1: Straight-line rate = 1/4 = 25%; DDB rate = 2 × 25% = 50% on the opening book value
Step 2: Year 1 depreciation = 50% × ₹80,000 = ₹40,000 → book value ₹40,000
Step 3: Year 2 depreciation = 50% × ₹40,000 = ₹20,000 → book value ₹20,000
Common mistake: Charging only one year (or straight line for two years) gives ₹40,000 (B). Applying the single 25% rate on WDV gives ₹80,000 × 0.75 × 0.75 = ₹45,000 (C). Charging 50% of COST each year gives nil (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — IF with AND
questions.question: A payroll sheet uses =IF(AND(B2>=25,C2>=5),"Bonus","No bonus"), where B2 holds an employee's age and C2 his years of service. If B2 = 30 and C2 = 4, the formula returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) No bonus
Step 1: B2 ≥ 25 → 30 ≥ 25 → TRUE
Step 2: C2 ≥ 5 → 4 ≥ 5 → FALSE
Step 3: AND(TRUE, FALSE) = FALSE → the IF returns the value_if_false part: 'No bonus'
Common mistake: Treating AND like OR gives 'Bonus' (A). TRUE (B) and 0 (C) are not what this IF returns — it returns one of the two text values.
Key point: AND needs ALL conditions true; OR needs ANY one.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — mixed cell references
questions.question: A rate table is built with the formula =$B2*C$1 entered in cell C2, so that it can be filled across and down. What will the formula read when it is copied from C2 into D3?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) =$B3*D$1
Why: In a mixed reference, the $ locks only the part it precedes. Moving one column right and one row down:
• $B2 → the column B is locked, the row is relative → $B3
• C$1 → the column is relative, the row 1 is locked → D$1
Why not the others:
(A) The row of $B2 should change to 3.
(C) $B cannot change to $C.
(D) The column of C$1 should change to D.
Key point: $ before the letter locks the column; $ before the number locks the row.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Features offered by electronic spreadsheet — data validation
questions.question: Which spreadsheet feature prevents a user from entering a value outside a permitted range — for example, a discount above 10% in a cell?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Data validation
Why: Data validation sets rules for what can be entered in a cell (number limits, dates, lists). Invalid entries are rejected, which reduces errors at the input stage.
Why not the others:
(A) Freeze panes keeps headings visible while scrolling.
(B) Conditional formatting changes how a cell looks based on its value, but does not stop an entry.
(D) A pivot table summarises data.
Key point: Prevent wrong input → data validation; highlight unusual values → conditional formatting.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: CAS — audit trail
questions.question: In a computerised accounting system, an 'audit trail' is:
options: A) A back-up copy of the company's data
B) The list of account codes in the chart of accounts
C) The final audited balance sheet
D) A record that traces each entry to its source, along with the user and the time of entry or change
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A record that traces each entry to its source, along with the user and the time of entry or change
Why: An audit trail logs who entered or altered a transaction and when. This lets auditors verify entries and detect unauthorised changes, and it is a key internal control in CAS.
Why not the others:
(A) A back-up is a safety copy of data.
(B) That is the chart of accounts.
(C) That is a financial statement.
Key point: Audit trail = traceability + accountability.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Reports generated by CAS
questions.question: In a computerised accounting system, which report lists the balances of all ledger accounts at a particular date, to check the arithmetical accuracy of the accounts?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Trial balance
Why: The trial balance lists the debit and credit balances of all ledger accounts. In CAS it is generated instantly from the posted vouchers, and its totals agree because every entry is posted with equal debits and credits.
Why not the others:
(B) A cash flow statement analyses cash movements by activity.
(C) A voucher is an input document.
(D) The chart of accounts lists account heads and codes, not balances.
Key point: Trial balance = list of ledger balances at a date.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Advantages of CAS
questions.question:
Which of the following are advantages of a computerised accounting system?
(A) Reports are available on time.
(B) It can handle a growing volume of transactions (scalability).
(C) It reduces errors in posting and totalling.
(D) It removes the need for any knowledge of accounting.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: NCERT lists the advantages of CAS as timely reports (A), scalability (B), accuracy because posting and totalling are automatic (C), and speed, reliability and real-time information.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the user must still understand accounting to classify transactions correctly and interpret the reports, because the software only processes what is entered. Options (A), (B) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: CAS automates processing, not accounting judgement.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Generating accounting information — SUMIF with a condition
questions.question: Cells B2:B6 contain the invoice values 4000, 6000, 5000, 8000 and 3000. The value returned by =SUMIF(B2:B6,">5000") is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 14000
Step 1: Values strictly greater than 5000: 6000 and 8000
Step 2: Sum = 6000 + 8000 = 14000 (when sum_range is omitted, the range itself is summed)
Common mistake: Including 5000 (as if the criterion were ">=5000") gives 19000 (A). Adding all the values gives 26000 (C). Counting the qualifying cells (=COUNTIF) gives 2 (D).
